a: Stoicism is an ancient Greek and Roman philosophy founded in Athens by Zeno of Citium around 300 BCE. It teaches that virtue (moral excellence) is the highest good and that the path to happiness is through accepting the present moment as it unfolds, focusing only on what is within our control, and not being controlled by the desire for pleasure or fear of pain. Central Stoic principles include: the Dichotomy of Control (focus on what you can control and accept what you cannot), living according to nature (understanding and aligning with the natural order of the universe), and the view that external events and circumstances are inherently neutral - it is our judgments about them that create suffering or peace. Key Stoic philosophers include Seneca (a Roman statesman and playwright), Epictetus (a former slave who became a respected teacher), and Marcus Aurelius (a Roman emperor whose Meditations remains a classic of Stoic thought). To apply Stoicism in daily life, you can practice negative visualization (imagining losing things you value to appreciate them more), journaling in the morning to prepare for challenges and in the evening to review your responses, focusing your energy only on what you can control, and reframing obstacles as opportunities for virtue. Modern applications of Stoicism include cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), which was influenced by Stoic ideas about how our beliefs shape our emotional responses.
